sk: ॐ सुकेशा च भारद्वाजः शैब्यश्च सत्यकामः सौर्यायणी च गार्ग्यः कौसल्यश्चाश्वलायनो भार्गवो वैदर्भिः कबन्धी कात्यायनस्ते हैते ब्रह्मपरा ब्रह्मनिष्ठाः परं ब्रह्मान्वेषमाणा एष ह वै तत्सर्वं वक्ष्यतीति ते ह समित्पाणयो भगवन्तं पिप्पलादमुपसन्नाः ||
ro: om · sukeśaḥ · ca · bhāradvājaḥ · śaibyaḥ · ca · satyakāmaḥ · sauryāyaṇī · ca · gārgyaḥ · kausalyaḥ · ca · āśvalāyanaḥ · bhārgavaḥ · vaidarbhiḥ · kabandhī · kātyāyanaḥ · te · ha · ete · brahma-parāḥ · brahma-niṣṭhāḥ · paraṁ · brahma · anveṣamāṇāḥ · eṣaḥ · ha · vai · tat · sarvaṁ · vakṣyati · iti · te · ha · samit-pāṇayaḥ · bhagavantaṁ · pippalādam · upasannāḥ ||
hi: ॐ। सुकेशा भारद्वाज, शैब्य सत्यकाम, सौर्यायणी गार्ग्य, कौसल्य आश्वलायन, भार्गव वैदर्भि, और कबन्धी कात्यायन — ये सब ब्रह्मपरायण (ब्रह्म में तत्पर), ब्रह्मनिष्ठ (ब्रह्म में स्थित), परम ब्रह्म के अन्वेषक (खोजने वाले) थे। (उन्होंने सोचा) 'यह (पिप्पलाद) निश्चय ही वह सब कुछ बताएँगे।' इसलिए वे समित्पाणि (हाथ में समिधा लिए) होकर भगवान् पिप्पलाद के पास उपसन्न (शिष्यभाव से उपस्थित) हुए।
en: Om. Sukesha Bhāradvāja, Shaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya, Kausalya Āshvalāyana, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi, and Kabandhī Kātyāyana — these, devoted to Brahman, established in Brahman, seeking the supreme Brahman, (thought:) 'He will indeed tell us all of That.' So, with fuel-sticks (samidh) in hand, they approached the venerable Pippalāda.

ws.h: ब्रह्म में तत्पर / ब्रह्म को सर्वोच्च मानने वाले
ws.e: devoted to Brahman — brahma (Brahman) + para (devoted to, intent on); those whose highest priority is Brahman-knowledge

ws.h: ब्रह्म में स्थित / ब्रह्म में दृढ़ निष्ठा वाले
ws.e: established in Brahman — brahma + niṣṭhā (steadfastness); not mere seekers but those already grounded in Brahman-practice
seeking / searching for — present participle of anu + √iṣ (to search); the active quest for the supreme
with fuel-sticks in hand — samidh (sacrificial firewood) + pāṇi (hand); the traditional sign of a student approaching a guru: bringing fuel for the sacred fire symbolises readiness to serve and learn
Pippalāda — the sage; name derived from pippala (the sacred fig/peepal berry); tradition says he survived on pippala fruits during austerities
approached (as students) — upa + √sad (to sit near); the formal act of approaching a teacher for instruction, sitting at his feet

gr: Six seekers are named, each from a different Vedic lineage (gotra): Bhāradvāja, Shaibya, Gārgya, Āshvalāyana, Vaidarbhi, Kātyāyana. The multiplicity of lineages signals that this teaching is universal — not restricted to one family or school. brahma-parāḥ brahma-niṣṭhāḥ — two qualifications: devotion to Brahman (aspiration) and steadfastness in Brahman (practice). They are not beginners but advanced seekers. samit-pāṇayaḥ — 'with fuel-sticks in hand': this is the ritual gesture of upanayana (formal studentship). The samidh is both practical (fuel for the guru's sacred fire) and symbolic (the student offers himself as fuel to be consumed in the fire of knowledge). upasannāḥ — 'approached': upa-√sad, the root of Upanishad itself ('sitting near'). The seekers enact the Upanishadic method: sit close to the master, serve, and receive.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.1 — The Prashna Upanishad belongs to the Atharva Veda and is structured as six questions (praśna) posed by six seekers to the sage Pippalāda. Each question opens a distinct topic. The name 'Pippalāda' connects to the pippala (sacred fig) tree — the same aśvattha tree central to the Katha (2.2.1) and Bhagavad Gītā (15.1). The six seekers represent six Vedic lineages, making this a pan-Vedic teaching. The structure — six questions, one teacher — distinguishes the Prashna from dialogue Upanishads like the Katha (one student, one teacher) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (multiple debates).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — छह शिष्य 'ब्रह्मपरा ब्रह्मनिष्ठा' हैं — अर्थात् वे अधिकारी (qualified) हैं। केवल अधिकारी ही ब्रह्मज्ञान प्राप्त कर सकता है। 'समित्पाणि' — यह विनय और सेवा-भाव का चिह्न है; ज्ञान विनम्र को ही प्राप्त होता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the six students are 'brahma-parā brahma-niṣṭhā' — meaning they are adhikārī (qualified). Only the qualified can receive Brahman-knowledge. 'Samit-pāṇi' — this signifies humility and readiness to serve; knowledge is granted only to the humble.
advaita.ins: Six seekers, six lineages, one question at each turn — the Upanishad is organised like a university seminar. But the prerequisite is not a degree; it is humility. You come with firewood, not credentials.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — छह शिष्यों का विविध गोत्रों से आना दिखाता है कि भगवद्-ज्ञान किसी एक वंश का एकाधिकार नहीं। 'ब्रह्मपरा' — जिनका लक्ष्य भगवान् हैं; 'समित्पाणि' — भक्ति-पूर्वक समर्पण का प्रतीक।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the six students coming from diverse lineages shows that knowledge of the Lord is not the monopoly of any one family. 'Brahma-parā' — those whose goal is the Lord; 'samit-pāṇi' — a symbol of devotional surrender.
vishisht.ins: The Lord's teaching is open to all lineages. No gotra owns the truth. Come with fuel for the fire, and the teacher will light it — whoever you are.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — छह शिष्य चेतना के विभिन्न पहलुओं (aspects) का प्रतिनिधित्व करते हैं — प्रत्येक एक भिन्न कोण से प्रश्न पूछता है। 'ब्रह्मनिष्ठा' — केवल बौद्धिक जिज्ञासा नहीं, अपितु साधना में प्रतिष्ठित होना।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees the six seekers as representing different aspects of consciousness — each asks from a different angle. 'Brahma-niṣṭhā' — not mere intellectual curiosity but being established in spiritual practice.
aurobindo.ins: Six seekers, six angles on the same truth. The Upanishad teaches that reality looks different depending on where you stand — but all views converge on the same centre.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the structure of the Prashna Upanishad?
dp.a: The Prashna Upanishad (from praśna = question) is structured as six questions posed by six seekers to the sage Pippalāda. Each question opens a distinct topic: Question 1 (Kabandhī): 'Whence are creatures born? What sustains them?' — the origin and sustenance of life through Prāṇa and Rayi (Matter and Energy). Question 2 (Bhārgava): 'How many gods support a creature? Which is chief?' — the hierarchy of bodily powers and the supremacy of Prāṇa. Question 3 (Kausalya): 'Whence is Prāṇa born? How does it enter the body?' — the origin, fivefold division, and functioning of the vital force. Question 4 (Sauryāyaṇī): 'What sleeps, what wakes, who sees dreams?' — the states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep). Question 5 (Shaibya): 'What is gained by meditating on OM?' — the significance and fruits of OM-meditation. Question 6 (Sukesha): 'Where is the sixteen-part Person?' — the supreme Puruṣa and the dissolution of the sixteen parts. The Upanishad belongs to the Atharva Veda and is one of the principal (mukhya) Upanishads commented upon by Shankara.

dp.q: 🔍 Why do the students bring fuel-sticks (samidh)?
dp.a: The samidh (sacrificial firewood) carried by approaching students is one of the oldest and most significant rituals in the Vedic tradition of knowledge-transmission. It operates on multiple levels: Practical: the student brings fuel for the guru's sacred fire (āhavanīya or gārhapatya agni). Maintaining the fire was a daily responsibility, and a student's contribution was his first act of service. Symbolic: the samidh represents the student himself — he offers himself as fuel to be consumed in the fire of knowledge. Just as wood is transformed into heat and light through fire, the student's ignorance is transformed into wisdom through the guru's teaching. Legal/ritual: carrying samidh is the formal gesture of upanayana — it signals the beginning of the guru-śiṣya relationship. The guru is not obligated to teach anyone who simply walks up; the samidh-bearing approach is a petition that the guru may accept or refuse. Ethical: the act of carrying firewood is an act of humility. The student, regardless of his social standing, performs a menial task. This establishes the relationship: the teacher is the fire, the student is the fuel. Without this humility, the Upanishad insists, knowledge cannot be transmitted.

sk: तान्ह स ऋषिरुवाच भूय एव तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण श्रद्धया संवत्सरं संवत्स्यथ यथाकामं प्रश्नान्पृच्छत यदि विज्ञास्यामः सर्वं ह वो वक्ष्यामः इति ||
ro: tān · ha · saḥ · ṛṣiḥ · uvāca · bhūyaḥ · eva · tapasā · brahmacaryeṇa · śraddhayā · saṁvatsaraṁ · saṁvatsyatha · yathā-kāmaṁ · praśnān · pṛcchata · yadi · vijñāsyāmaḥ · sarvaṁ · ha · vaḥ · vakṣyāmaḥ · iti ||
hi: उन (शिष्यों) से उस ऋषि (पिप्पलाद) ने कहा — 'एक संवत्सर (वर्ष) और तपस्या, ब्रह्मचर्य और श्रद्धा के साथ निवास करो। फिर यथाकाम (इच्छानुसार) प्रश्न पूछो। यदि हम जानते होंगे, तो सब कुछ तुम्हें बताएँगे।'
en: The sage said to them: 'Dwell here for one more year, with austerity (tapas), celibacy (brahmacharya), and faith (śraddhā). Then ask questions as you wish. If we know, we shall tell you everything.'

ws.e: with austerity — tapas (heat/austerity, from √tap, to heat); the inner fire of self-discipline that purifies the mind
with celibacy / continence — brahma + carya (conduct befitting Brahman); the student's discipline of sexual restraint and devoted study
with faith — śrad (heart) + √dhā (to place); placing one's heart in the teaching and the teacher; trust that precedes and enables understanding
for one year — the traditional probationary period; the student must prove readiness through sustained discipline before receiving teaching
as you wish — yathā (as) + kāma (desire); after the year, they may ask freely, without restriction
if we shall know — the sage's humility: 'if I know the answer' (even the greatest teacher does not claim omniscience)

gr: bhūyaḥ eva — 'even more / further': the seekers are already qualified (brahma-niṣṭhā), but Pippalāda asks for more preparation. Knowledge has prerequisites beyond mere aspiration. Three prerequisites: tapas (austerity — purification of will), brahmacarya (celibacy/continence — conservation of vital energy), śraddhā (faith — trust in the teaching before it is understood). saṁvatsaram — 'for one year': the waiting period is not arbitrary; it tests sincerity, patience, and readiness. yadi vijñāsyāmaḥ — 'if we shall know': the sage's extraordinary humility — he does not guarantee answers. Even Pippalāda defers to truth: 'I will teach only what I truly know.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.2 — The three prerequisites (tapas, brahmacarya, śraddhā) appear across multiple Upanishads. The Muṇḍaka (1.2.12-13) similarly requires the student to approach 'samit-pāṇiḥ śrotriyaṁ brahma-niṣṭham' — 'with fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned and established in Brahman.' The one-year waiting period is a standard feature of guru-śiṣya protocol (cf. Chāndogya 4.4 — Satyakāma Jābāla's years of service). The sage's 'yadi vijñāsyāmaḥ' (if we know) is a hallmark of Vedic intellectual humility — the teacher claims mastery only over what he has personally realised.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — तप, ब्रह्मचर्य और श्रद्धा — ये तीन अन्तःकरण-शुद्धि (inner purification) के साधन हैं। बिना शुद्ध अन्तःकरण के ब्रह्मज्ञान सम्भव नहीं। एक वर्ष — यह काल-सीमा शिष्य की दृढ़ता की परीक्षा है।
advaita.en: Shankara says tapas, brahmacarya, and śraddhā are the three means of antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi (inner purification). Without a purified inner instrument, Brahman-knowledge is impossible. One year — this time-frame tests the student's resolve.
advaita.ins: The teacher does not test your intelligence — he tests your patience. A year of austerity, celibacy, and faith is not a punishment; it is a preparation. A mirror must be cleaned before it can reflect.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — तप = भगवान् के लिए कष्ट सहना; ब्रह्मचर्य = इन्द्रिय-संयम; श्रद्धा = गुरु और शास्त्र में अचल विश्वास। 'यदि विज्ञास्यामः' — यह ऋषि की विनम्रता है; सच्चा गुरु कभी सर्वज्ञता का दावा नहीं करता।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says tapas = enduring hardship for the Lord; brahmacarya = sense-control; śraddhā = unwavering faith in the guru and scriptures. 'If we know' — this is the sage's humility; a true guru never claims omniscience.
vishisht.ins: The greatest teacher says 'if I know.' Not because he doubts, but because truth is greater than any teacher. He will not invent answers — he will share only what he has seen.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — तीन शर्तें तीन स्तरों पर कार्य करती हैं: तप = इच्छा-शक्ति का शोधन (purification of will); ब्रह्मचर्य = प्राण-शक्ति का संरक्षण (conservation of vital energy); श्रद्धा = मानसिक खुलापन (mental receptivity)। ये तीनों मिलकर चेतना को ज्ञान-ग्रहण के योग्य बनाते हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the three conditions operate at three levels: tapas = purification of will; brahmacarya = conservation of vital energy; śraddhā = mental receptivity. Together they prepare consciousness to receive knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: Knowledge does not enter a closed container. Tapas opens the will, brahmacarya gathers the energy, śraddhā opens the mind. A year of this triple preparation makes you a vessel — and the teacher can finally pour.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does Pippalāda demand a year of waiting?
dp.a: The one-year waiting period serves multiple purposes in the Vedic guru-śiṣya tradition: (1) Testing sincerity: anyone can ask a question; only the truly committed will wait a year for the answer. The waiting separates serious seekers from casual inquirers. (2) Purification: the year is spent in tapas (austerity), brahmacarya (continence), and śraddhā (faith) — three disciplines that purify the antaḥkaraṇa (inner instrument) so it can receive and hold the teaching. An impure vessel cannot hold pure water. (3) Building relationship: the guru-śiṣya relationship is not transactional (ask → answer). It is transformational — the student must live with the teacher, serve him, observe his conduct, absorb his presence. A year of close proximity allows the student to absorb not just the teacher's words but his being. (4) Maturation: some truths cannot be heard until the student has matured. The year allows questions to deepen — what you ask after a year of contemplation is different from what you would have asked on day one. The Chāndogya Upanishad provides parallels: Satyakāma Jābāla tends cattle for years before receiving teaching (4.4-9); Upakosala Kāmālayana maintains the sacred fires for twelve years (4.10). The waiting is not arbitrary — it is the teaching.

dp.q: 🔍 What do tapas, brahmacarya, and śraddhā mean?
dp.a: These three prerequisites appear repeatedly across the Upanishads as the conditions for receiving knowledge: Tapas (from √tap, 'to heat/burn'): literally 'heat' — the inner fire generated by self-discipline, austerity, and sustained effort. Tapas burns away impurities of will: laziness, distraction, attachment to comfort. It is not punishment but purification by fire. The Muṇḍaka (1.2.11) calls it 'tapas + śraddhā' — the twin pillars. Brahmacarya (brahma + carya, 'conduct befitting Brahman'): primarily sexual continence, but more broadly the conservation of vital energy. In the Vedic understanding, sexual energy (vīrya/ojas) and intellectual clarity are connected. Brahmacarya redirects vital energy from reproduction to realisation. It also means 'student conduct' — the entire mode of life of one devoted to learning: simplicity, discipline, service. Śraddhā (śrad + √dhā, 'placing the heart'): faith — but not blind belief. Śraddhā is the willingness to trust the teaching and the teacher before complete understanding arrives. It is the bridge between hearing a truth and realising it. Without śraddhā, the student's intellect becomes a wall rather than a door — endlessly analysing, never entering. The Gītā (4.39) affirms: 'śraddhāvāl labhate jñānam' — 'the faithful one attains knowledge.'

sk: अथ कबन्धी कात्यायन उपेत्य पप्रच्छ | भगवन्कुतो ह वा इमाः प्रजाः प्रजायन्ते इति ||
ro: atha · kabandhī · kātyāyanaḥ · upetya · papraccha | bhagavan · kutaḥ · ha · vā · imāḥ · prajāḥ · prajāyante · iti ||
hi: अब (एक वर्ष के बाद) कबन्धी कात्यायन ने (पिप्पलाद के) पास जाकर पूछा — 'भगवन्! ये प्रजाएँ (जीव/प्राणी) कहाँ से उत्पन्न होती हैं?'
en: Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana, having approached, asked: 'Bhagavan! From where are these creatures born?'

ws.e: Kabandhī Kātyāyana — the first questioner; from the Kātyāyana lineage (descendants of sage Katyāyana)
having approached — upa + √i (to go); the formal approach to the teacher for a specific question
asked — perfect tense of √prach (to ask); the formal, reverent asking
creatures are born — prajā (progeny/creatures) + pra-√jan (to be born forth); the question about the origin of all living beings

gr: atha — 'then': marks the transition from the probationary period to the teaching proper. The year of preparation is over. upetya papraccha — 'having approached, he asked': the formal sequence — first approach with reverence, then ask. kutaḥ imāḥ prajāḥ prajāyante — 'from where are these creatures born?': the first question is cosmogonic — not 'who am I?' but 'where does everything come from?' This is the most fundamental question: the origin of existence itself. The verb prajāyante (are born forth) uses the same root as prajā (creatures/progeny), creating an etymological echo: 'whence do the born-forth ones become born-forth?'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.3 — The first question is cosmogonic — it asks about the origin of all creatures. This parallels the Rig Vedic Nāsadīya Sūkta (10.129): 'ko addhā veda ka iha pra vocat / kuta ājātā kuta iyaṁ visṛṣṭiḥ' — 'Who truly knows? Who can say from where this creation arose?' The Prashna's answer will involve Prāṇa (life-force) and Rayi (matter), a distinctive framework not found in other Upanishads.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह प्रश्न सृष्टि-विद्या (cosmogony) का है। 'कुतः प्रजायन्ते' — सृष्टि का मूल कारण क्या है? शंकर इसे अध्यारोप-अपवाद (superimposition-removal) दृष्टि से देखते हैं — सृष्टि ब्रह्म पर अध्यारोपित है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this is a question about cosmogony (sṛṣṭi-vidyā). 'Whence are they born?' — what is the root cause of creation? Shankara reads it through the lens of adhyāropa-apavāda (superimposition-removal) — creation is superimposed on Brahman.
advaita.ins: The first question is the most basic: where does everything come from? Until you answer this, every other question hangs in the air.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'कुतः प्रजायन्ते' — भगवान् से; सृष्टि भगवान् की इच्छा (saṅkalpa) से होती है। यह प्रश्न भगवान् की सृजन-शक्ति को जानने का प्रथम चरण है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'whence are they born?' — from the Lord; creation arises from the Lord's will (saṅkalpa). This question is the first step in knowing the Lord's creative power.
vishisht.ins: Before you can know the Creator, you must first wonder about creation. The first question is always: who made all this? And the answer always points to the Lord.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — यह प्रश्न चेतना के प्रकटीकरण (manifestation) के बारे में है: जीवन कहाँ से आता है? उत्तर — प्राण (life-force) और रयि (matter) — चेतना और ऊर्जा के दो ध्रुव हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads this as a question about the manifestation of consciousness: where does life come from? The answer — Prāṇa (life-force) and Rayi (matter) — represents the two poles of consciousness and energy.
aurobindo.ins: Where does life come from? This is not an academic question — it is the most personal question there is. You are alive; you did not choose to be. Where did this life come from?

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the origin of creatures the first question?
dp.a: The question 'kutaḥ prajāḥ prajāyante' (whence are creatures born?) is placed first because it is the most fundamental cosmological question. Before asking about the soul, consciousness, meditation, or liberation, one must first understand: what is this world, and where did it come from? This ordering follows a natural philosophical sequence: (1) Origin of the world (Question 1), (2) Structure of the individual (Questions 2-3), (3) States of consciousness (Question 4), (4) Means of liberation (Question 5), (5) The ultimate reality (Question 6). The Prashna moves from outside to inside, from cosmos to Self. This mirrors the Vedic approach: the Rig Vedic hymns begin with cosmic questions (creation hymns, Nāsadīya Sūkta 10.129) before moving to self-inquiry. The question also has a personal dimension: 'where do creatures come from?' is also 'where did I come from?' Every individual's existence presupposes a cosmic process. Understanding that process is the first step toward understanding oneself within it.

dp.q: 🔍 Who is Kabandhī Kātyāyana?
dp.a: Kabandhī Kātyāyana is the first of the six seekers to pose his question. His name connects him to the Kātyāyana lineage — descendants of the sage Katyāyana, one of the most prominent families in the Vedic intellectual tradition. Kātyāyana is associated with the Śukla Yajur Veda and is credited with important contributions to Vedic ritual science (the Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra). The name 'Kabandhī' may derive from kabandha (a headless trunk, or a large mass), possibly indicating a clan or sub-lineage name. His question — about the origin of creatures — is the most external and cosmic of the six questions, appropriate for the opening. In the Prashna's carefully graded sequence, the questions move progressively inward: from cosmic origin (Q1) through the body's powers (Q2-3), states of consciousness (Q4), meditation technique (Q5), to the ultimate Self (Q6). By asking the 'outermost' question, Kabandhī establishes the framework within which all subsequent, more inward questions make sense.

sk: तस्मै स होवाच प्रजाकामो ह वै प्रजापतिः स तपोऽतप्यत स तपस्तप्त्वा स मिथुनमुत्पादयते | रयिं च प्राणं चेत्येतौ मे बहुधा प्रजाः करिष्यत इति ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · prajā-kāmaḥ · ha · vai · prajāpatiḥ · saḥ · tapaḥ · atapyata · saḥ · tapaḥ · taptvā · saḥ · mithunam · utpādayate · rayiṁ · ca · prāṇaṁ · ca · iti · etau · me · bahudhā · prajāḥ · kariṣyataḥ · iti ||
hi: उनसे वह (पिप्पलाद) बोले — 'प्रजाकाम (सन्तान / सृष्टि की इच्छा रखने वाले) प्रजापति ने तप किया। तप करके उन्होंने एक मिथुन (युगल / जोड़ा) उत्पन्न किया — रयि (पदार्थ / चन्द्रमा-तत्त्व) और प्राण (जीवन-शक्ति / सूर्य-तत्त्व)। (उन्होंने सोचा) 'ये दोनों मेरे लिए बहुत प्रकार की प्रजाएँ उत्पन्न करेंगे।'
en: To him he (Pippalāda) said: 'Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerity (tapas). Having performed tapas, he produced a pair (mithuna) — Rayi (matter/moon-principle) and Prāṇa (life-force/sun-principle). (He thought:) These two will produce manifold creatures for me.'

ws.e: desiring offspring — prajā (progeny) + kāma (desire); Prajāpati's will to create is the primordial impulse behind the universe
the Lord of Creatures — prajā (creatures) + pati (lord); the cosmic creator-principle in Vedic cosmology
a pair / couple — from √mith (to unite); creation requires polarity — two complementary principles working together
Rayi — matter/substance/moon-principle; from √rī (to flow); the material, receptive, nourishing aspect of creation
Prāṇa — life-force/sun-principle; the energising, activating, consciousness aspect of creation

gr: prajā-kāmaḥ prajāpatiḥ — 'Prajāpati, desiring offspring': creation is not accidental but intentional — it arises from desire (kāma). This echoes the Rig Veda (10.129.4): 'kāmas tad agre samavartatādhi manaso retaḥ prathamaṁ yad āsīt' — 'Desire arose in the beginning, the first seed of the mind.' tapas atapyata — 'he performed tapas': creation through tapas (creative heat) is the standard Vedic cosmogonic model. mithunam utpādayate — rayiṁ ca prāṇaṁ ca — 'he produced a pair — Rayi and Prāṇa': this is the Prashna's distinctive cosmology. All creation results from the interaction of two complementary principles: Rayi (matter/substance/the receptive) and Prāṇa (energy/life-force/the active). This is not identical to Sāṅkhya's puruṣa-prakṛti but shares the structural insight that reality requires polarity.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.4 — The Prāṇa-Rayi cosmology is unique to the Prashna Upanishad. Rayi (from √rī, 'to flow') = matter, substance, the moon-principle, the receptive, the feminine. Prāṇa = energy, life-force, the sun-principle, the active, the masculine. This binary framework parallels but predates Sāṅkhya's puruṣa-prakṛti (consciousness-matter) dualism. The Rig Vedic cosmogonic hymn (10.129) also begins with desire (kāma) and tapas as the origin of creation. Prajāpati as creator is the standard Brāhmaṇa-era cosmology (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.1.1.1).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्रजापति = ईश्वर (सगुण ब्रह्म); तप = संकल्प-शक्ति (creative will)। रयि-प्राण = नाम-रूप (name-and-form) — माया के दो पहलू। सृष्टि ब्रह्म में अध्यारोपित है; वास्तव में ब्रह्म अपरिवर्तित रहता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Prajāpati = Īśvara (saguṇa Brahman); tapas = creative will (saṅkalpa-śakti). Rayi-Prāṇa = name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) — two aspects of māyā. Creation is superimposed on Brahman; Brahman itself remains unchanged.
advaita.ins: Creation is not a labour — it is a thought. Prajāpati's tapas is not effort but intention. The universe arises because the Absolute willed it — and that will split into two: energy and matter, sun and moon, life and form.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्रजापति = भगवान् नारायण का सृजन-रूप। रयि और प्राण = भगवान् की दो शक्तियाँ — चित् (चेतन) और अचित् (जड़)। भगवान् इच्छा (संकल्प) से सृष्टि करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prajāpati = Lord Nārāyaṇa's creative aspect. Rayi and Prāṇa = the Lord's two powers — cit (conscious) and acit (inert). The Lord creates by will (saṅkalpa).
vishisht.ins: The universe is born from a pair — matter and life, body and breath. But behind the pair stands the Lord, who made them and set them to work together.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — रयि = पदार्थ/ऊर्जा का ग्राहक (receptive) पक्ष; प्राण = चेतना का सक्रिय (active) पक्ष। सृष्टि इन दो ध्रुवों के बीच की अन्तर्क्रिया (interaction) है — जैसे विद्युत् में धन और ऋण ध्रुव।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads Rayi as the receptive aspect of energy/matter and Prāṇa as the active aspect of consciousness. Creation is the interaction between these two poles — like positive and negative poles of electricity.
aurobindo.ins: The universe runs on polarity — not opposition but complementarity. Life needs form, form needs life. Sun needs moon, energy needs matter. Creation is the dance between these two partners.

dp.q: 🔍 What are Prāṇa and Rayi?
dp.a: The Prashna Upanishad's Prāṇa-Rayi framework is its most distinctive cosmological contribution. Prāṇa (from pra + √an, 'to breathe forth') is the life-force, energy, the active principle, the sun-principle. It is the power that animates, that gives movement and consciousness to matter. In subsequent verses, Prāṇa is identified with the sun (āditya), fire (agni), and the masculine principle. Rayi (from √rī, 'to flow') is matter, substance, the receptive principle, the moon-principle. It is what receives the animation of Prāṇa, what takes form and gives body. In subsequent verses, Rayi is identified with the moon (soma/candra), food (anna), and the feminine principle. The key insight: neither principle alone can create. Prāṇa without Rayi is formless energy; Rayi without Prāṇa is inert matter. Creation requires their union (mithuna). This binary framework anticipates several later systems: Sāṅkhya's puruṣa-prakṛti (consciousness and matter); Tantra's Śiva-Śakti (static consciousness and dynamic energy); Chinese philosophy's yang-yin; and even modern physics' energy-matter duality.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Vedic cosmogony understand creation?
dp.a: Vedic cosmogony offers multiple, complementary models of creation — not contradicting each other but illuminating different aspects: (1) Desire + Tapas model (this verse, Rig Veda 10.129): creation arises from desire (kāma) — the Absolute's wish to become many — followed by tapas (creative heat/austerity). Desire provides direction; tapas provides power. (2) Speech/Word model (Rig Veda 10.71, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.2): creation through vāc (speech/word) — the Absolute utters the cosmos into being. 'In the beginning was the Word.' (3) Sacrifice model (Puruṣa Sūkta, Rig Veda 10.90): the cosmic Puruṣa is sacrificed, and from his dismembered body the world arises — the four varṇas from his limbs, the elements from his faculties. (4) Emanation model (Taittirīya 2.1, Muṇḍaka 1.1.7): creation flows forth from Brahman as sparks from fire, web from spider, hair from body — Brahman is the material AND efficient cause. (5) Polarity model (this Upanishad): creation requires a pair — Prāṇa and Rayi, energy and matter, active and receptive. None of these models claims exclusivity; the Vedic tradition views creation as too vast for any single explanation. Each model captures one dimension of the mystery.

sk: आदित्यो ह वै प्राणो रयिरेव चन्द्रमा रयिर्वा एतत्सर्वं यन्मूर्तं चामूर्तं च तस्मान्मूर्तिरेव रयिः ||
ro: ādityaḥ · ha · vai · prāṇaḥ · rayiḥ · eva · candramāḥ · rayiḥ · vā · etat · sarvaṁ · yat · mūrtaṁ · ca · amūrtaṁ · ca · tasmāt · mūrtiḥ · eva · rayiḥ ||
hi: आदित्य (सूर्य) ही प्राण है; रयि निश्चय ही चन्द्रमा है। जो कुछ मूर्त (साकार) और अमूर्त (निराकार) है — यह सब रयि है। इसलिए मूर्ति (आकार/रूप) ही रयि है।
en: The sun (Āditya) indeed is Prāṇa; the moon (Chandra) indeed is Rayi. All this that has form (mūrta) and that which is formless (amūrta) — all that is Rayi. Therefore, form itself is Rayi.

ws.e: the sun — Āditya (son of Aditi); here identified with Prāṇa: the sun is the cosmic source of life-energy
the moon — identified with Rayi: the moon represents reflected light, receptivity, the material/nourishing principle
having form — from √mūrch (to solidify); anything with a definite shape or material embodiment
formless — a + mūrta; without definite shape; even formless substances (air, space, energy-fields) are classified as Rayi
form — the principle of taking shape; wherever there is form, there is Rayi

gr: ādityaḥ ha vai prāṇaḥ — 'the sun indeed is Prāṇa': the cosmic identification. The sun is not merely a symbol of Prāṇa — it IS Prāṇa at the cosmic level. The sun is the source of all energy, warmth, and life in the physical universe — exactly what Prāṇa is at the metaphysical level. rayiḥ eva candramāḥ — 'Rayi indeed is the moon': the moon receives and reflects the sun's light — it is the receptive principle. In Vedic thought, the moon is also connected to soma (the nourishing, sustaining substance) and to food (anna). mūrtaṁ ca amūrtaṁ ca — 'both the formed and the formless': Rayi includes everything that has substance, whether shaped (mūrta) or unshaped (amūrta). Even formless things (like wind or space) are Rayi if they are material (as opposed to conscious). mūrtiḥ eva rayiḥ — 'form itself is Rayi': the principle is generalised — wherever there is form, there is Rayi.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.5 — The sun-moon / Prāṇa-Rayi identification is the Prashna's central cosmological insight. In Vedic cosmology, the sun (Āditya) is the source of all life — 'sūrya ātmā jagatas tasthuṣaś ca' (Rig Veda 1.115.1) — 'The sun is the Self of all that moves and stands.' The moon (Soma/Candra) is the source of nourishment and the repository of the dead (pitṛloka is often associated with the moon). The mūrta-amūrta distinction parallels the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's (2.3.1) division of Brahman into two forms: 'dve vāva brahmaṇo rūpe — mūrtaṁ caivāmūrtaṁ ca.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सूर्य = प्राण (चेतन शक्ति); चन्द्रमा = रयि (जड़ पदार्थ)। मूर्त-अमूर्त — दोनों रयि (नाम-रूप) हैं। प्राण (चेतना) रयि (पदार्थ) से भिन्न है — यही सृष्टि का मूल द्वैत है, जो अंततः ब्रह्म में एक है।
advaita.en: Shankara says sun = Prāṇa (conscious power); moon = Rayi (inert matter). Both formed and formless are Rayi (name-and-form). Prāṇa (consciousness) is distinct from Rayi (matter) — this is the fundamental duality of creation, ultimately unified in Brahman.
advaita.ins: Look at the world and see two things: the energy that animates, and the matter that takes shape. The sun gives life; the moon gives form. Between them, everything exists.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सूर्य = भगवान् की चेतन शक्ति (चित्); चन्द्रमा = भगवान् की जड़ शक्ति (अचित्)। दोनों भगवान् के शरीर (body) हैं — चित् और अचित् दोनों भगवान् में आश्रित हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says sun = the Lord's conscious power (cit); moon = the Lord's inert power (acit). Both are the Lord's body — cit and acit both depend on the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Everything you see is the Lord's body — the living and the lifeless, the shining and the still. Sun and moon are His two hands, energy and matter His two expressions.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — सूर्य-चन्द्रमा = चेतना और ऊर्जा के दो ध्रुव। सूर्य = चैतन्य-शक्ति (conscious force); चन्द्रमा = ग्राहक पदार्थ (receptive substance)। मूर्त-अमूर्त — सब 'रयि' है — चेतना का ग्राहक माध्यम।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads sun-moon as two poles of consciousness and energy. Sun = conscious force; moon = receptive substance. Both formed and formless are Rayi — the receptive medium of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The sun pours out force; the moon receives and shapes it. This is the cosmic breathing — an exhalation of energy, an inhalation of form. The universe lives between these two breaths.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the sun identified with Prāṇa?
dp.a: The identification of Āditya (sun) with Prāṇa (life-force) is one of the oldest Vedic insights. The Rig Veda (1.115.1) declares: 'sūrya ātmā jagatas tasthuṣaś ca' — 'The sun is the Self (ātmā) of all that moves and all that stands still.' In the physical world, the sun is the source of all energy: photosynthesis depends on sunlight, weather systems are driven by solar energy, the food chain begins with the sun's rays. Without the sun, life on earth would cease. The Prashna extends this physical observation into metaphysics: just as the physical sun energises the physical world, Prāṇa (the cosmic life-force) energises the subtle world — it is the power that animates all beings, that makes matter alive. The identification is not metaphorical but structural: the sun is Prāṇa's cosmic form, and Prāṇa is the sun's essential nature. At the individual level, the prāṇa in your body (your breath, your vital force) is a portion of the cosmic Prāṇa that manifests as the sun. When you breathe, you are participating in the same energy that makes the sun shine.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the mūrta-amūrta distinction?
dp.a: The mūrta-amūrta (formed-formless) distinction is a fundamental classification in Vedic ontology. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upanishad (2.3.1) makes it explicit: 'dve vāva brahmaṇo rūpe — mūrtaṁ caivāmūrtaṁ ca, martyaṁ cāmṛtaṁ ca, sthitaṁ ca yac ca, sac ca tyac ca' — 'There are indeed two forms of Brahman — the formed and the formless, the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and the moving, the real and the beyond.' Mūrta (from √mūrch, 'to solidify'): anything with a definite form — earth, water, bodies, objects. Amūrta (formless): anything without definite form — air, space, fire, energy. The Prashna's innovation is to classify both mūrta and amūrta as Rayi. Even formless substances (air, energy-fields, space) are material — they belong to the receptive side of creation, not the conscious side. Prāṇa alone is the conscious principle; everything else — whether it has form or not — is Rayi (matter in the broadest sense). This anticipates modern physics' insight that energy and matter are interconvertible (E=mc²): both are aspects of the same 'substance' — what the Prashna calls Rayi.

sk: अथादित्य उदयन्यत्प्राचीं दिशं प्रविशति तेन प्राच्यान्प्राणान्रश्मिषु सन्निधत्ते | यद्दक्षिणां यत्प्रतीचीं यदुदीचीं यदधो यदूर्ध्वं यदन्तरा दिशो यत्सर्वं प्रकाशयति तेन सर्वान्प्राणान्रश्मिषु सन्निधत्ते ||
ro: atha · ādityaḥ · udayan · yat · prācīṁ · diśaṁ · praviśati · tena · prācyān · prāṇān · raśmiṣu · sannidhatte | yat · dakṣiṇāṁ · yat · pratīcīṁ · yat · udīcīṁ · yat · adhaḥ · yat · ūrdhvaṁ · yat · antarā · diśaḥ · yat · sarvaṁ · prakāśayati · tena · sarvān · prāṇān · raśmiṣu · sannidhatte ||
hi: अब, सूर्य उदय होकर जब पूर्व दिशा में प्रवेश करता है, तो अपनी किरणों (रश्मियों) में पूर्व दिशा के प्राणों (जीवों) को सन्निहित (समाहित/ग्रहण) करता है। जब दक्षिण, पश्चिम, उत्तर, अधः (नीचे), ऊर्ध्व (ऊपर), और अन्तर (मध्य) दिशाओं को — सब कुछ प्रकाशित करता है — तो अपनी किरणों में सभी प्राणों को सन्निहित करता है।
en: Now, when the sun rises and enters the eastern direction, it gathers the living beings (prāṇas) of the east into its rays. When it illumines the south, the west, the north, below, above, and the intermediate quarters — when it illumines everything — it gathers all living beings into its rays.

ws.e: rising — present participle of ud + √i (to go up); the sun rising
the eastern direction — prācī (eastern) + diś (direction/quarter)
in the rays — locative plural of raśmi (ray/beam of light); the sun's rays are the medium through which Prāṇa energises all beings

ws.h: सन्निहित करता है / समाहित करता है / ग्रहण करता है
ws.e: gathers / holds together / sustains — sam + ni + √dhā (to place); the sun 'holds' all beings in its rays, i.e., sustains their life-force
illumines everything — the sun's light reaches all directions without exception

gr: ādityaḥ udayan — 'the sun rising': the description follows the sun's journey across the sky — east at dawn, then sweeping through all directions. This is not mere astronomy; it is a cosmological statement about Prāṇa's universal reach. raśmiṣu sannidhatte — 'gathers in its rays': the sun's rays are not merely light — they are the conduits of Prāṇa. Every ray carries life-force. When the sun shines on a being, it is not just illuminating it but sustaining it. The enumeration of all directions — east, south, west, north, below, above, intermediate — is a totality formula. It means: there is no direction the sun does not reach. Therefore: there is no being Prāṇa does not sustain.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.6 — The sun's rays as conduits of Prāṇa is a distinctive Prashna teaching. The Chāndogya (3.1-11) similarly describes the sun's rays as 'honey-channels' connecting the sun to different directions and Vedic texts. The idea that the sun 'gathers' (sannidhatte) all beings in its rays echoes the Rig Vedic understanding of the sun as the cosmic eye (sūrya cakṣuḥ) that 'sees' (and thereby sustains) all beings. The Gāyatrī mantra (RV 3.62.10) invokes this sun-principle: 'tat savitur vareṇyaṁ bhargo devasya dhīmahi' — 'we meditate on the glorious light of the divine Savitṛ.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सूर्य की किरणें प्राण-शक्ति की वाहक हैं। सूर्य सर्वव्यापी प्रकाश = ब्रह्म का सर्वव्यापी चैतन्य। जैसे सूर्य सब दिशाओं को प्रकाशित करता है, वैसे ब्रह्म सब प्राणियों को चेतना देता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the sun's rays are carriers of Prāṇa-śakti. The sun's all-pervading light = Brahman's all-pervading consciousness. As the sun illumines all directions, Brahman gives consciousness to all beings.
advaita.ins: The sun does not choose whom to shine on. Its light falls on saint and sinner, mountain and valley, palace and hovel. That is the nature of Prāṇa — it sustains all, without discrimination.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सूर्य भगवान् की प्राण-शक्ति का प्रतीक है। भगवान् की कृपा सूर्य-किरणों की भाँति सर्वत्र पहुँचती है — कोई दिशा, कोई प्राणी उससे वंचित नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the sun symbolises the Lord's Prāṇa-śakti. The Lord's grace, like the sun's rays, reaches everywhere — no direction, no being is excluded.
vishisht.ins: The Lord's sustaining power is like the sun that shines in all directions. You cannot escape it — and why would you want to? Every breath you take is a ray of His grace.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — सूर्य = चेतना-शक्ति (consciousness-force) जो अपनी 'किरणों' (rays of influence) से सब कुछ व्याप्त करती है। यह चेतना का सर्वव्यापी प्रसार (all-pervading radiation) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads the sun as consciousness-force that pervades everything through its 'rays' (influences). This is the all-pervading radiation of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is not confined to the brain. Like the sun's rays, it reaches everywhere — into every cell, every atom, every direction. The Upanishad is describing a universe saturated with awareness.

dp.q: 🔍 How does the sun sustain all life?
dp.a: The verse describes the sun as gathering all living beings into its rays (raśmiṣu sannidhatte). This operates at multiple levels: Physical: the sun is the ultimate source of energy for all life on earth. Photosynthesis converts sunlight into plant matter; plants feed herbivores; herbivores feed carnivores. Remove the sun, and the entire food chain collapses. The sun's heat drives weather, ocean currents, and the water cycle. In a very literal sense, all life is 'sustained' by the sun's rays. Vedic-cosmological: in the Vedic worldview, the sun is not merely a ball of plasma but the cosmic eye (sūrya cakṣuḥ) — the organ through which the cosmic intelligence perceives and sustains the world. The Gāyatrī mantra (RV 3.62.10) invokes the sun's inner light: 'tat savitur vareṇyaṁ bhargo devasya dhīmahi' — 'we meditate on the glorious splendour of the divine Savitṛ.' This 'splendour' (bhargas) is not just physical light but consciousness-light. Metaphysical: the sun = Prāṇa. Prāṇa is the life-principle — that which makes matter alive. The sun's rays are the medium through which Prāṇa reaches all beings. When sunlight touches a plant, it is Prāṇa entering matter (Rayi) and creating life.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the significance of naming all directions?
dp.a: The enumeration of all directions — east, south, west, north, below, above, and the intermediate quarters — is a Vedic totality formula. It means: without exception, in every possible direction. This is not geographic but metaphysical: Prāṇa reaches everywhere. No corner of the universe is outside its reach. The six main directions (pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, uttara, adhaḥ, ūrdhva) define the three-dimensional spatial framework. The 'intermediate quarters' (antarā diśaḥ) fill in the diagonals (northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest). Together, they form the complete spatial sphere — every point in space is covered. This totality formula appears frequently in Vedic literature: it is a way of saying 'absolutely everything, without remainder.' By stating that the sun illumines ALL directions, the Upanishad is saying that Prāṇa sustains ALL beings — not just some, not just the worthy, not just those in certain locations. The life-force is universal. This is both a cosmological fact (the sun shines everywhere) and a spiritual insight (consciousness pervades all).

sk: स एष वैश्वानरो विश्वरूपः प्राणोऽग्निरुदयते | तदेतदृचाऽभ्युक्तम् ||
ro: saḥ · eṣaḥ · vaiśvānaraḥ · viśva-rūpaḥ · prāṇaḥ · agniḥ · udayate | tat · etat · ṛcā · abhyuktam ||
hi: वही यह वैश्वानर (सब मनुष्यों/प्राणियों में व्याप्त), विश्वरूप (सर्वरूप), प्राण-रूपी अग्नि उदय होता है। यही ऋचा (ऋग्वेद-मन्त्र) द्वारा कहा गया है —
en: This same one — the Vaishvānara (universal fire), the one of universal form (vishvarūpa), Prāṇa as fire — rises. This has been declared by the Rig Vedic verse:

ws.h: वैश्वानर — सर्वमानवीय / सब प्राणियों में व्याप्त अग्नि
ws.e: the universal fire — viśva (all) + nara (men); the fire that is common to all beings; also the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) in the body
of universal form — viśva (all) + rūpa (form); having every form, present in all shapes and manifestations
fire — Prāṇa manifests as Agni (fire); fire is the visible form of the life-force: it consumes, transforms, and energises
declared by a Ṛg verse — ṛc (Rig Vedic verse) + abhyukta (spoken about); introducing a scriptural citation

gr: vaiśvānaraḥ — 'the universal fire': this term bridges the cosmic and the individual. At the cosmic level, Vaiśvānara is the fire that pervades all creation. At the individual level, it is the jaṭharāgni (digestive fire) that burns in every belly — transforming food into energy. The Bhagavad Gītā (15.14) echoes: 'ahaṁ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṁ deham āśritaḥ' — 'I, becoming Vaiśvānara, dwell in the bodies of living beings.' viśva-rūpaḥ — 'of universal form': Prāṇa does not have one form — it has all forms. It appears as sun, fire, wind, breath, and the life-force in every creature. ṛcā abhyuktam — 'declared by a Rig verse': Pippalāda cites Vedic authority for his teaching — the next verse is the citation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.7 — The identification Prāṇa = Agni = Vaiśvānara links three major Vedic concepts. Vaiśvānara appears in the Rig Veda (1.98.1, 3.2.1), the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, and the Chāndogya (5.11-24, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā). The Bhagavad Gītā (15.14) directly echoes this: 'ahaṁ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṁ deham āśritaḥ / prāṇāpāna-samāyuktaḥ pacāmy annaṁ catur-vidham' — 'Becoming Vaiśvānara, I dwell in the body, united with prāṇa and apāna, and digest the four kinds of food.' The 'ṛcā abhyuktam' (declared by a Rig verse) introduces the citation in the next mantra.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — वैश्वानर = सार्वभौम चेतना जो अग्नि-रूप में प्रकट होती है। प्राण = अग्नि = ब्रह्म-शक्ति — सब एक ही सत्ता के विभिन्न नाम हैं। 'विश्वरूप' — ब्रह्म सर्वरूप है, किसी एक रूप में सीमित नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says Vaiśvānara = universal consciousness manifesting as fire. Prāṇa = Agni = Brahman's power — all are different names of the same reality. 'Viśvarūpa' — Brahman is of all forms, not limited to any one.
advaita.ins: The fire in your belly and the fire in the sun are the same fire. The breath in your lungs and the wind in the sky are the same breath. One Prāṇa, infinite forms.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'वैश्वानर' = भगवान् का अग्नि-रूप; गीता (15.14) में भगवान् स्वयं कहते हैं 'अहं वैश्वानरो भूत्वा' — 'मैं वैश्वानर बनकर शरीर में निवास करता हूँ।' प्राण = भगवान् की जीवन-शक्ति।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'Vaiśvānara' = the Lord's fire-form; in the Gītā (15.14) the Lord Himself says 'I, becoming Vaiśvānara, dwell in the body.' Prāṇa = the Lord's life-force.
vishisht.ins: When you eat and the food is digested, that is the Lord working in you. He is not somewhere far away — He is the fire in your stomach, the warmth in your blood, the breath in your chest.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — वैश्वानर = सार्वभौम अग्नि-शक्ति (universal fire-force) जो पदार्थ को रूपांतरित करती है। प्राण-अग्नि = चेतना की वह शक्ति जो जड़ पदार्थ में प्रवेश करके उसे जीवित करती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads Vaiśvānara as the universal fire-force that transforms matter. Prāṇa-Agni = the power of consciousness that enters inert matter and makes it alive.
aurobindo.ins: Life is fire — not destruction but transformation. The fire in every cell converts food into energy, matter into consciousness. That is the cosmic Agni at work in your body.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the Vaiśvānara fire?
dp.a: Vaiśvānara (from viśva + nara, 'universal man' or 'common to all men') is one of the most important fire-concepts in Vedic thought. It operates at three levels: (1) Cosmic: Vaiśvānara is the fire-principle that pervades the entire universe — the energy that sustains all creation. The sun is its most visible form. (2) Individual: Vaiśvānara is the jaṭharāgni (digestive fire) in every living being. The Bhagavad Gītā (15.14) identifies it explicitly: 'ahaṁ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṁ deham āśritaḥ / prāṇāpāna-samāyuktaḥ pacāmy annaṁ catur-vidham' — 'I, becoming Vaiśvānara, dwell in the body of living beings; united with prāṇa and apāna, I digest the four kinds of food.' (3) Ritual: Vaiśvānara is the sacrificial fire — the fire on the altar through which offerings reach the gods. The Chāndogya Upanishad (5.11-24) develops the Vaiśvānara-vidyā at length: it describes the cosmic Vaiśvānara whose head is heaven, whose eyes are the sun and moon, whose breath is the wind, whose body is space, whose bladder is water, and whose feet are the earth. The Prashna's contribution is to identify Vaiśvānara with Prāṇa — the life-force is the fire, and the fire is the life-force.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Prāṇa relate to Agni (fire)?
dp.a: The equation Prāṇa = Agni is one of the Prashna Upanishad's central identifications. Fire (Agni) and life-force (Prāṇa) share fundamental properties: (1) Both transform: fire transforms fuel into heat and light; Prāṇa transforms food into life-energy. Digestion is literally 'burning' food with the body's fire. (2) Both sustain: without fire, the world would be cold and dark; without Prāṇa, beings would be dead and inert. (3) Both pervade: fire exists in hidden form in all substances (latent heat, molecular energy); Prāṇa exists in all living beings. (4) Both ascend: fire always rises; Prāṇa's upward flow (udāna) carries consciousness upward at death (as taught in Question 3). The Rig Veda's very first word is 'agnim' (fire) — the first hymn invokes Agni as the mediator between humans and gods. The Prashna extends this: Agni-Prāṇa is the mediator between Rayi (matter) and consciousness. Fire enters matter and makes it alive — that is Prāṇa's function at every scale, from the cosmic sun to the digestive flame.

sk: विश्वरूपं हरिणं जातवेदसं परायणं ज्योतिरेकं तपन्तम् | सहस्ररश्मिः शतधा वर्तमानः प्राणः प्रजानामुदयत्येष सूर्यः ||
ro: viśva-rūpaṁ · hariṇaṁ · jāta-vedasaṁ · parāyaṇaṁ · jyotiḥ · ekaṁ · tapantam | sahasra-raśmiḥ · śatadhā · vartamānaḥ · prāṇaḥ · prajānām · udayati · eṣaḥ · sūryaḥ ||
hi: विश्वरूप (सर्वरूप), हरिण (सुवर्ण-वर्ण / हरण करने वाला), जातवेदस् (सब जन्मों/वस्तुओं को जानने वाला), परायण (परम आश्रय), एक ज्योति (एकमात्र प्रकाश), तपन्तम् (तपाने वाला), सहस्ररश्मि (हजारों किरणों वाला), शतधा वर्तमानः (सैकड़ों प्रकार से प्रवृत्त) — यही प्रजाओं (जीवों) का प्राण है — यही सूर्य उदय होता है।
en: Of universal form, golden, all-knowing (jātavedas), the supreme goal, the one light, the one who gives warmth — with a thousand rays, existing in a hundred ways — this, the Prāṇa of all creatures, is the sun that rises.

ws.h: हरिण — सुवर्ण-वर्ण / हरित / हरण करने वाला
ws.e: golden / tawny — from √hṛ (to take away); also 'the one who draws/attracts all things'; the sun's golden colour

ws.h: जातवेदस् — सब जातों (जन्मों/प्राणियों) को जानने वाला
ws.e: the all-knowing — jāta (born/created) + vedas (knowledge); Agni/Sūrya as the one who knows all that is born; a standard Vedic epithet of fire
the supreme refuge/goal — para (highest) + ayana (abode/path); the ultimate destination of all beings
the one light — there is only one source of illumination; all other lights derive from this
thousand-rayed — sahasra (thousand) + raśmi (ray); denoting infinite emanation of light and life
existing in a hundred ways — śatadhā (in a hundred ways) + vartamāna (existing); Prāṇa manifests diversely throughout creation

gr: This is a Rig Vedic citation — Pippalāda quotes Vedic authority to validate his Prāṇa-Sūrya identification. viśva-rūpam — 'of universal form': repeated from the previous verse, creating an anaphoric link. hariṇam — 'golden/tawny': the sun's colour, but also from √hṛ (to take/attract) — the sun 'draws' all beings toward itself. jāta-vedasam — 'the all-knowing': one of Agni's most important Vedic epithets, appearing from the first hymn (RV 1.1.1: agniṁ ... jātavedasam). It means both 'knower of all that is born' and 'one in whom all beings find their knowledge.' prāṇaḥ prajānām udayati eṣaḥ sūryaḥ — 'this sun rises as the Prāṇa of all creatures': the climactic identification — the sun = the Prāṇa of all life.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.8 — This verse is a Rig Vedic citation (though not traceable to a single extant Rig Vedic hymn in its current form — it may be from a lost recension or a composite). The epithet 'jātavedas' links back to Agni's role from RV 1.1.1 onward. The identification sūryaḥ = prāṇaḥ prajānām ('the sun is the life-force of all creatures') is the doctrinal climax of the Prāṇa-sun equation established in mantras 5-7. 'Sahasra-raśmiḥ' (thousand-rayed) echoes the Puruṣa Sūkta (RV 10.90.1): 'sahasra-śīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt' — the thousand-headed, thousand-eyed Puruṣa.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह वैदिक प्रमाण है: सूर्य = प्राण = ब्रह्म-शक्ति। 'एकं ज्योति' — प्रकाश एक ही है; सूर्य, चन्द्रमा, तारे, अग्नि — सब उसी एक ज्योति के प्रतिबिम्ब हैं। 'सहस्ररश्मि' — एक से अनेक; ब्रह्म से विश्व।
advaita.en: Shankara says this is Vedic authority: sun = Prāṇa = Brahman's power. 'One light' — there is only one source of luminosity; sun, moon, stars, fire are all reflections of that one light. 'Thousand-rayed' — from one to many; from Brahman to the universe.
advaita.ins: There is only one light in the universe, wearing a thousand masks. The sun, the candle, the firefly, the thought that illuminates your mind — all one light, all one Prāṇa.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सूर्य भगवान् का दीप्तिमान् स्वरूप है — 'परायणम्' (परम आश्रय) = भगवान् ही अंतिम शरणागति हैं। 'जातवेदस्' = जो सब प्राणियों को जानता है — यह सर्वज्ञता भगवान् की है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the sun is the Lord's radiant form — 'parāyaṇam' (supreme refuge) = the Lord alone is the ultimate shelter. 'Jātavedas' = the one who knows all beings — this omniscience belongs to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The sun knows every blade of grass it shines on. The Lord knows every creature He sustains. You are never unknown, never unseen, never unfelt.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — यह मन्त्र चेतना-शक्ति (consciousness-force) का वैदिक स्तुतिगान है। 'सहस्ररश्मि' — एक चेतना अनन्त किरणों में विकीर्ण होती है। 'ज्योतिरेकम्' — सब ज्ञान, सब प्रकाश एक ही स्रोत से आता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads this as a Vedic hymn to consciousness-force. 'Thousand-rayed' — one consciousness radiates in infinite rays. 'One light' — all knowledge, all illumination comes from one source.
aurobindo.ins: A thousand rays, but one sun. A hundred forms, but one Prāṇa. The whole diversity of life is the sunlight of consciousness playing on the waters of matter.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'jātavedas' mean?
dp.a: Jātavedas is one of the most important epithets of Agni (Fire) in the Rig Veda — it appears from the very first hymn (RV 1.1.1). The word has two primary etymologies: (1) jāta + vedas = 'knower of all that is born' — Agni/Sūrya as the omniscient witness of all creation. Nothing is born or dies without fire's knowledge. In every birth, the fire of life is kindled; in every death, it is extinguished. (2) jāta + vedas = 'one in whom all that is born finds its knowledge' — Agni as the repository of all knowledge. All beings find their truth in the cosmic fire. The epithet is significant because it personalises fire — Agni is not a blind force but a knower. The fire that burns in the universe is not merely physical energy; it is intelligent energy — consciousness in its most active, transformative form. In the Prashna's context, applying 'jātavedas' to the sun-as-Prāṇa means: the life-force that sustains all beings is not a mechanical process — it is a conscious sustaining. The universe is maintained by knowing energy, not by blind force.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the sun called 'the one light' (jyotiḥ ekam)?
dp.a: The declaration 'jyotiḥ ekam' (the one light) makes a claim that goes far beyond astronomy: there is only one source of illumination in the universe. All other lights — the moon, stars, fire, lightning — are either reflections or derivatives of this one light. This echoes the Katha Upanishad (2.2.15): 'na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakaṁ nemā vidyuto bhānti kuto 'yam agniḥ / tam eva bhāntam anubhāti sarvaṁ tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṁ vibhāti' — 'There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars, nor these lightnings — how then this fire? Everything shines after That which shines; by Its light all this shines.' The Muṇḍaka (2.2.10) echoes identically. The philosophical implication: the light of consciousness is the one true light. Physical light (photons, electromagnetic radiation) is a derivative of the consciousness-light (cit-jyoti). The mind's ability to perceive light is prior to light itself — without consciousness, light would exist but have no witness, no meaning. The Prashna identifies this consciousness-light with Prāṇa-as-Sūrya: the sun is the physical expression of the one consciousness-light that illuminates all reality.

sk: संवत्सरो वै प्रजापतिस्तस्यायने दक्षिणं चोत्तरं च | तद्ये ह वै तदिष्टापूर्ते कृतमित्युपासते ते चान्द्रमसमेव लोकमभिजयन्ते | त एव पुनरावर्तन्ते तस्मादेत ऋषयः प्रजाकामा दक्षिणं प्रतिपद्यन्ते | एष ह वै रयिर्यः पितृयाणः ||
ro: saṁvatsaraḥ · vai · prajāpatiḥ · tasya · ayane · dakṣiṇaṁ · ca · uttaraṁ · ca | tat · ye · ha · vai · tat · iṣṭā-pūrte · kṛtam · iti · upāsate · te · cāndramasam · eva · lokam · abhijayante | te · eva · punaḥ · āvartante · tasmāt · ete · ṛṣayaḥ · prajā-kāmāḥ · dakṣiṇaṁ · pratipadyante | eṣaḥ · ha · vai · rayiḥ · yaḥ · pitṛ-yāṇaḥ ||
hi: संवत्सर (वर्ष) ही प्रजापति है; उसके दो अयन (मार्ग) हैं — दक्षिणायन और उत्तरायण। जो 'इष्टापूर्त' (यज्ञ और पुण्य-कर्म) ही कृत (किया) है — ऐसा मानकर उपासना करते हैं, वे चान्द्रमस लोक (चन्द्रलोक) को जीतते हैं। वे पुनः लौटते हैं (पुनर्जन्म लेते हैं)। इसलिए ये ऋषि जो प्रजाकाम (सन्तान की इच्छा वाले) हैं, दक्षिणायन (दक्षिण मार्ग) का आश्रय लेते हैं। यही रयि है — यह पितृयाण (पितरों का मार्ग) है।
en: The year (saṁvatsara) indeed is Prajāpati; it has two paths — the southern (dakṣiṇāyana) and the northern (uttarāyaṇa). Those who worship thinking 'we have performed sacrifice and merit' — they win only the world of the moon. They return again (are reborn). Therefore those sages who desire offspring take the southern path. This indeed is Rayi — the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa).

ws.e: the year — the complete annual cycle; identified with Prajāpati because the year is the cosmic cycle through which creation proceeds
paths/courses — the two halves of the solar year: dakṣiṇāyana (sun moving south, June-December) and uttarāyaṇa (sun moving north, January-June)
sacrifice and merit — iṣṭa (Vedic fire-sacrifices) + pūrta (meritorious works like digging wells, building temples); the two categories of ritual-based religious activity
the world of the moon — the celestial realm reached by meritorious ritualists; temporary, not permanent liberation

ws.h: पुनः लौटते हैं / पुनर्जन्म लेते हैं
ws.e: they return again — punaḥ (again) + ā + √vṛt (to turn); the key limitation: this path leads back to rebirth when merit is exhausted
the path of the fathers — the route by which the soul travels after death through the moon-realm and back to rebirth; contrasted with the devayāna (path of the gods)

gr: saṁvatsaraḥ vai prajāpatiḥ — 'the year is Prajāpati': time itself is the creator. The annual cycle — with its seasons, solstices, and rhythms — is the mechanism of creation. dakṣiṇaṁ ca uttaraṁ ca — the two 'ayanas' (paths/courses): the dakṣiṇāyana (southern course, when the sun moves south) and the uttarāyaṇa (northern course, when the sun moves north) divide the year into two cosmic directions. iṣṭā-pūrte kṛtam iti upāsate — 'they worship thinking: we have done sacrifice and merit': these are ritualists who rely solely on karma-kāṇḍa (ritual action) without jñāna (knowledge). te cāndramasam eva lokam abhijayante — 'they win only the moon-world': the reward is real but temporary. punaḥ āvartante — 'they return': the devastating limitation. This is the Upanishadic critique of mere ritualism.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.9 — The two paths (devayāna and pitṛyāṇa) are taught extensively in the Chāndogya (5.10) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15-16). The pitṛyāṇa: death → smoke → night → dark fortnight → dakṣiṇāyana → moon → rain → earth → food → seed → rebirth. The devayāna: death → flame → day → bright fortnight → uttarāyaṇa → sun → lightning → Brahman (no return). The Prashna's innovation is to correlate these paths with Rayi (pitṛyāṇa = matter-path = return) and Prāṇa (devayāna = life-force-path = liberation). Bhīṣma in the Mahābhārata waited for uttarāyaṇa before dying (MB 6.119), based on this doctrine.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — केवल कर्मकाण्ड (ritual action) से चन्द्रलोक (स्वर्ग) मिलता है, पर वह अनित्य है — पुण्य-क्षय होने पर पुनर्जन्म होता है। 'रयि' = पितृयाण = भौतिक पथ — यह चक्र (cycle) है, मुक्ति नहीं। केवल ज्ञान से मुक्ति।
advaita.en: Shankara says mere ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa) earns only the moon-world (heaven), which is impermanent — when merit is exhausted, rebirth follows. 'Rayi' = pitṛyāṇa = the material path — this is a cycle, not liberation. Only knowledge liberates.
advaita.ins: Ritual without knowledge is a round trip. You ascend to heaven on the fuel of merit; when the fuel burns out, you fall back. The only one-way ticket is knowledge.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — पितृयाण = कर्म-प्रधान उपासक; वे भगवान् की शरणागति के बिना कर्मफल भोगकर लौटते हैं। उत्तरायण/देवयान = भक्ति-प्रधान उपासक; वे भगवान् तक पहुँचकर कभी नहीं लौटते।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says pitṛyāṇa = karma-dominant worshippers; without surrender to the Lord, they enjoy merit and return. Uttarāyaṇa/devayāna = bhakti-dominant worshippers; they reach the Lord and never return.
vishisht.ins: Two roads lead out of this life. One circles back; the other goes straight to the Lord. The difference? On the first, you rely on your own merit. On the second, you rely on His grace.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'पितृयाण' = पदार्थ-प्रधान (matter-dominant) पथ — चेतना रयि (matter) की ओर उन्मुख रहती है; इसलिए पुनर्जन्म होता है। 'देवयान' = चेतना-प्रधान पथ — चेतना प्राण (consciousness-force) की ओर उन्मुख होती है; इसलिए मुक्ति।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads pitṛyāṇa as the matter-dominant path — consciousness oriented toward Rayi (matter), hence rebirth. Devayāna as the consciousness-dominant path — consciousness oriented toward Prāṇa, hence liberation.
aurobindo.ins: You always travel toward what you worship. If you worship results (merit, heaven, rewards), you get results — and they run out. If you worship the source, you reach the source — and it never runs out.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the two paths — devayāna and pitṛyāṇa?
dp.a: The doctrine of the two paths is one of the most important teachings in the Upanishads, developed in detail in the Chāndogya (5.10) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15-16). Pitṛyāṇa (path of the fathers): the soul after death travels through: smoke → night → dark fortnight → dakṣiṇāyana (southern course) → the moon → rain → earth → food → seed → rebirth. This path is for those whose spiritual practice is karma-dominant — they perform sacrifices and good works but lack transformative knowledge. Their merit earns them a temporary stay in the moon-world (candraloka), but when the merit is exhausted, they return to earthly existence. Devayāna (path of the gods): the soul after death travels through: flame → day → bright fortnight → uttarāyaṇa (northern course) → the sun → lightning → Brahman → no return. This path is for those whose practice includes jñāna (knowledge) or upāsanā (meditation on Brahman). They reach Brahman and do not return. The Prashna correlates these paths with its own framework: pitṛyāṇa = Rayi (the material principle), devayāna = Prāṇa (the conscious principle). The path you travel after death corresponds to what you worshipped in life: matter or consciousness.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the Upanishad critique ritualism?
dp.a: The phrase 'iṣṭā-pūrte kṛtam iti upāsate' ('they worship thinking: we have done sacrifice and merit') is a pointed critique of mere ritualism. The Upanishad does not reject ritual — it rejects ritual without knowledge. The critique operates on several levels: (1) Temporal limitation: ritual merit (puṇya) produces real results — heaven, prosperity, good rebirth — but these results are temporary. When the merit is exhausted, the soul returns. This is like a bank account: you can deposit virtue, but eventually you spend it all. (2) Structural limitation: ritual operates within the domain of Rayi (matter, the moon-principle). It produces effects within the material world — better worlds, better bodies — but cannot take you beyond the material world. For that, you need Prāṇa (consciousness, the sun-principle) — which means knowledge. (3) Psychological limitation: the ritualist thinks 'kṛtam iti' — 'I have done it.' This sense of 'I am the doer, I have earned this' is itself a form of bondage. Liberation requires the dissolution of the doer-identity, not its glorification. The Upanishadic position is not anti-ritual but pro-knowledge: ritual is valuable as preparation for knowledge (it purifies the mind) but not as a substitute for it.

sk: अथोत्तरेण तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण श्रद्धया विद्ययाऽऽत्मानमन्विष्यादित्यमभिजयन्ते | एतद्वै प्राणानामायतनमेतदमृतमभयमेतत्परायणमेतस्मान्न पुनरावर्तन्त इत्येष निरोधस्तदेष श्लोकः ||
ro: atha · uttareṇa · tapasā · brahmacaryeṇa · śraddhayā · vidyayā · ātmānam · anviṣya · ādityam · abhijayante | etat · vai · prāṇānām · āyatanam · etat · amṛtam · abhayam · etat · parāyaṇam · etasmāt · na · punaḥ · āvartante · iti · eṣaḥ · nirodhaḥ · tat · eṣaḥ · ślokaḥ ||
hi: अब (दूसरा मार्ग —) उत्तरायण (उत्तर मार्ग) द्वारा, तपस्या, ब्रह्मचर्य, श्रद्धा और विद्या (ज्ञान) से आत्मा को खोजकर, वे आदित्य (सूर्य) को जीतते हैं। यही प्राणों का आयतन (निवास-स्थान) है; यही अमृत (अमर) है; यही अभय (भय-रहित) है; यही परायण (परम आश्रय) है। इससे वे पुनः नहीं लौटते — यही निरोध (अवरोध / रुकना) है। यही श्लोक (उक्ति) है —
en: But by the northern path, through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge (vidyā), having sought the Self, they win the sun (Āditya). This indeed is the abode of all prāṇas; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is the supreme refuge. From this they do not return — this is the cessation (nirodha). On this, here is a verse:

ws.e: by the northern (path) — the uttarāyaṇa; the path of the gods (devayāna) leading to non-return
by knowledge — vidyā (spiritual knowledge, specifically ātma-vidyā); the critical addition to the three prerequisites of tapas, brahmacarya, śraddhā
having sought the Self — anu + √iṣ (to seek); active pursuit of Self-knowledge through inquiry and meditation
they win/conquer the sun — they reach the realm of Prāṇa (the sun-principle) and attain immortality
the abode / resting-place — ā + √yat (to rest in); the sun is where all individual prāṇas originate and return
cessation / stoppage — ni + √rudh (to obstruct); the cessation of the cycle of rebirth; the stopping-point of transmigration

gr: uttareṇa — 'by the northern path': contrasted with dakṣiṇa (south) in the previous verse. North = up = light = liberation; south = down = darkness = return. vidyayā — 'by knowledge': this is the crucial addition. The previous verse listed only ritual (iṣṭā-pūrta); this verse adds vidyā (knowledge of the Self). The four prerequisites — tapas, brahmacarya, śraddhā, vidyā — form the complete path. ātmānam anviṣya — 'having sought the Self': the active ingredient — not passive receipt of merit but active search for the Self. na punaḥ āvartante — 'they do not return': the definitive mark of liberation. nirodhaḥ — 'cessation': a term later central to Yoga philosophy (Yoga Sūtra 1.2: yogaḥ citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ); here it means the cessation of the cycle of rebirth.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.10 — The contrast between mantras 9 and 10 is the doctrinal core of Question 1: pitṛyāṇa (ritual alone → return) vs. devayāna (knowledge + ritual → no return). The addition of 'vidyā' (knowledge) to the prerequisites is the differentiating factor. The term 'nirodha' here prefigures Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra (1.2): 'yogaḥ citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ' — yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. The Bhagavad Gītā (8.24) specifies the uttarāyaṇa path: 'agniḥ jyotiḥ ahaḥ śuklaḥ ṣaṇ-māsā uttarāyaṇam / tatra prayātā gacchanti brahma brahma-vido janāḥ.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'विद्या' ही निर्णायक अंतर है: तप + ब्रह्मचर्य + श्रद्धा + विद्या = देवयान (अपुनरावृत्ति); बिना विद्या = पितृयाण (पुनरावृत्ति)। 'निरोध' = संसार-चक्र का सदा के लिए अवरोध। 'आदित्य' = ब्रह्म — सूर्य-प्रतीक।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'vidyā' is the decisive difference: tapas + brahmacarya + śraddhā + vidyā = devayāna (no return); without vidyā = pitṛyāṇa (return). 'Nirodha' = permanent cessation of the saṁsāra cycle. 'Āditya' = Brahman — symbolised by the sun.
advaita.ins: Add one ingredient to your spiritual practice and everything changes: knowledge. Without it, all your austerity and faith earn you a holiday in heaven — and then the holiday ends. With it, you never come back.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'विद्या' = भगवत्-ज्ञान और भक्ति; 'आदित्य' = भगवान् का तेजोमय स्वरूप। 'न पुनरावर्तन्ते' — भगवान् के धाम से कोई नहीं लौटता; यह भगवान् की कृपा की शाश्वतता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'vidyā' = knowledge of the Lord and devotion; 'Āditya' = the Lord's radiant form. 'They do not return' — no one returns from the Lord's abode; this is the eternal nature of the Lord's grace.
vishisht.ins: Knowledge of the Lord is the passport that has no return stamp. Once you enter His light, you stay. Not because you cannot leave, but because there is nowhere else to go.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'विद्या' = आत्म-ज्ञान; 'आदित्य' = चेतना का सूर्य (supramental light)। 'निरोध' = निम्न प्रकृति (lower nature) के चक्र का अन्त — चेतना अपने दिव्य स्रोत में प्रतिष्ठित हो जाती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads 'vidyā' as Self-knowledge; 'Āditya' as the sun of consciousness (supramental light). 'Nirodha' = the end of the cycle of lower nature — consciousness establishes itself in its divine source.
aurobindo.ins: The difference between circling and arriving is knowledge. The ritualist circles — each orbit brings him back to the same place. The knower arrives — at the sun, the source, the place from which there is no departure because there is no distance left to travel.

dp.q: 🔍 What makes the devayāna path irreversible?
dp.a: The devayāna ('path of the gods') leads to non-return (apunar-āvṛtti) because it is based on vidyā (knowledge) rather than merely on karma (action). The critical difference: Karma produces finite results. Every action generates a specific, measurable merit (puṇya). Merit is like fuel — it is consumed in the process of producing its result. When the merit of a good life is 'used up' in the moon-world (enjoying heavenly pleasures), there is nothing left to sustain the soul there, and it falls back to earth. This is the pitṛyāṇa. Vidyā produces an infinite result. Knowledge is not consumed in use. Once you know that fire burns, you cannot 'use up' this knowledge. Once you know the Self, this knowledge does not deplete. It transforms the knower permanently. The transformation is irreversible — like carbon becoming diamond, the structure has changed at the fundamental level. Furthermore: karma reinforces the sense of doership ('I did this, I earned this'), which is the root of bondage. Vidyā dissolves the doer-identity ('there is no separate I; all is Brahman'), which is liberation itself. You cannot 'return' from this because there is no 'you' separate from Brahman to do the returning. The Bhagavad Gītā (8.16) confirms: 'ā-brahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar-āvartino 'rjuna / mām upetya tu kaunteya punar-janma na vidyate' — 'All worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return; but having reached Me, there is no rebirth.'

dp.q: 🔍 What is the meaning of 'nirodha' here?
dp.a: The word nirodha (ni + √rudh, 'to obstruct/stop') means cessation — here, the cessation of the cycle of rebirth. The soul that reaches the sun (Āditya) via the devayāna path stops — the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth comes to a permanent halt. This is significant because the term 'nirodha' later becomes central to Yoga philosophy. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra (1.2) defines yoga as 'yogaḥ citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ' — 'yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind-stuff.' In Buddhism, nirodha (cessation of duḥkha/suffering) is the Third Noble Truth. In all three contexts — Upanishadic, Yogic, and Buddhist — nirodha means the stopping of an unwanted process: in the Prashna, the stopping of rebirth; in Yoga, the stopping of mental fluctuations; in Buddhism, the stopping of suffering. The Prashna's usage is the earliest of these and may represent the archetype from which the later technical usages developed. The implication: liberation is not something you get — it is something that stops. Saṁsāra is an ongoing process; liberation is its cessation.

sk: पञ्चपादं पितरं द्वादशाकृतिं दिव एहुः परे अर्धे पुरीषिणम् | अथेमे अन्य उ परे विचक्षणं सप्तचक्रे षडर आहुरर्पितमिति ||
ro: pañca-pādaṁ · pitaraṁ · dvādaśa-ākṛtiṁ · divaḥ · ehuḥ · pare · ardhe · purīṣiṇam | atha · ime · anye · u · pare · vicakṣaṇaṁ · sapta-cakre · ṣaḍ-araḥ · āhuḥ · arpitam · iti ||
hi: (कुछ ज्ञानी) कहते हैं — (वह प्रजापति/काल) पञ्चपाद (पाँच ऋतुओं वाला), पिता, द्वादशाकृति (बारह रूपों/महीनों वाला) है; वह दिव (आकाश) के ऊपर के अर्ध (आधे भाग) में पुरीषिन् (जल-दाता / वर्षा करने वाला) है। अन्य (दूसरे विद्वान्) कहते हैं — वह विचक्षण (सर्वद्रष्टा) सप्तचक्र (सात चक्रों / पहियों वाले रथ) में छह अरों (six spokes) पर स्थापित है।
en: Some say He (Prajāpati/Time) has five feet (seasons), is the father, has twelve forms (months), and is the rain-giver in the upper half of heaven. Others say He, the all-seeing, is placed in a chariot of seven wheels with six spokes.

ws.e: five-footed — pañca (five) + pāda (foot); the five seasons (vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemanta-śiśira counted together, or the five visible seasons)
twelve-formed — dvādaśa (twelve) + ākṛti (form); the twelve months of the year
the rain-giver — purīṣa (water/rain); the cosmic process that brings rain from the upper atmosphere
in a seven-wheeled (chariot) — the seven wheels may represent the seven chandas (Vedic metres) or the seven planes of existence
six-spoked — ṣaṭ (six) + ara (spoke); the six seasons (ṛtus), or six categories of beings

gr: This is a highly compressed cosmological verse — almost a riddle — describing Prajāpati (the year/time) through numerical symbolism. pañca-pādam — 'five-footed': the year as five seasons (the ancient Vedic count: vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemanta-śiśira combined). dvādaśa-ākṛtim — 'twelve-formed': the twelve months. purīṣiṇam pare ardhe divaḥ — 'the rain-giver in the upper half of heaven': the cosmic process of rain, which sustains all life, originates from the upper atmosphere. sapta-cakre ṣaḍ-are — 'seven-wheeled, six-spoked': the year as a cosmic chariot — seven wheels (perhaps the seven days of the week, or seven chandas/metres) and six spokes (perhaps six seasons, or six categories of beings). This verse has strong Rig Vedic parallels (RV 1.164).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_1.11 — This verse is closely related to the great cosmological riddle-hymn of the Rig Veda (1.164), the Asya Vāmasya Sūkta by Dīrghatamas. RV 1.164.12: 'pañca-pādaṁ pitaram dvādaśākṛtiṁ diva āhuḥ pare ardhe purīṣiṇam / atheme anye upare vicakṣaṇaṁ saptacakre ṣaḍara āhur arpitam.' The Prashna quotes this virtually verbatim. The Rig Vedic original describes the cosmic year-wheel — the sun's annual journey mapped onto a chariot. The numbers encode calendrical data: 12 months, 5 (or 6) seasons, 7 days/metres, 360 (6 × 60) days.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — यह काल (Time) का वर्णन है — प्रजापति = काल। पाँच पाद = पाँच ऋतुएँ; बारह आकृति = बारह मास; सात चक्र = सात छन्द (गायत्री आदि) या सप्तलोक। यह श्लोक ऋग्वेद (1.164) से उद्धृत है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this describes Time (Kāla) — Prajāpati = Time. Five feet = five seasons; twelve forms = twelve months; seven wheels = seven chandas (metres) or seven worlds. This verse is cited from the Rig Veda (1.164).
advaita.ins: Time is a chariot with seven wheels and twelve forms. You are riding in it right now. The question is not whether you can stop the chariot — you cannot. The question is whether you can see who is driving.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — यह भगवान् का काल-रूप (time-form) है — ऋतुएँ, मास, सप्ताह — सब भगवान् की लीला (play) का ताल (rhythm) है। 'पिता' — भगवान् सृष्टि के पिता हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says this is the Lord's time-form — seasons, months, weeks are the rhythm (tāla) of the Lord's play (līlā). 'Father' — the Lord is the father of creation.
vishisht.ins: Time is not an enemy — it is the rhythm of the Lord's dance. The seasons are His steps, the months His gestures. To see time as the Lord's movement is to stop fearing it.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — यह ऋग्वैदिक कूट-श्लोक (riddle-verse) है — सृष्टि-चक्र को रथ-रूपक में प्रस्तुत करता है। सात चक्र = सात चेतना-स्तर (planes of consciousness); छह अरे = छह ऊर्जा-केन्द्र (चक्र)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo reads this as a Rig Vedic riddle-verse presenting the creation-cycle as a chariot metaphor. Seven wheels = seven planes of consciousness; six spokes = six energy-centres (chakras).
aurobindo.ins: The cosmos is a riddle wrapped in numbers. Five seasons, twelve months, seven wheels, six spokes — each number is a key. The Vedic seers hid their deepest truths in numbers, knowing that only the attentive would decode them.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the Rig Vedic riddle-hymn (1.164)?
dp.a: This verse is a near-verbatim quotation from the Asya Vāmasya Sūkta (Rig Veda 1.164), attributed to the seer Dīrghatamas Aucathya ('Long Darkness, son of Ucathya'). This is one of the most enigmatic and celebrated hymns in the Rig Veda — a 52-verse riddle-poem describing the cosmos through numerical symbolism. The hymn contains many famous verses: the 'two birds on one tree' (1.164.20), the cosmic wheel (1.164.11-13), and the 'speech has four quarters' (1.164.45: 'catvāri vāk parimitā padāni'). The numbers in this verse encode calendrical and cosmic data: 5 feet = 5 seasons (or 5 years of the Vedic yuga-cycle); 12 forms = 12 months; 7 wheels = 7 days of the week, or 7 Vedic metres (gāyatrī, uṣṇik, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, paṅkti, triṣṭubh, jagatī), or 7 lokas; 6 spokes = 6 seasons (ṛtus), or 360 days grouped in 6 sets of 60. The Prashna's citation of this archaic hymn is significant: it anchors the Upanishadic teaching in the oldest Vedic authority.

dp.q: 🔍 How does time relate to Prajāpati?
dp.a: The identification saṁvatsaraḥ vai prajāpatiḥ ('the year is Prajāpati') is fundamental to Vedic cosmology. Prajāpati (Lord of Creatures) is the creator-principle — and the year is the mechanism through which creation operates. Creation is not a single event but an ongoing process governed by temporal cycles: the daily cycle (sunrise-sunset), the monthly cycle (moon phases), the annual cycle (seasons), the cosmic cycle (yugas). Time IS creation: without the passage of time, nothing would be born, grow, decay, or die. The year — with its seasons, months, and days — is the body of time, and Prajāpati is its soul. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (6.1.1.1 ff.) develops this extensively: 'Prajāpati desired: may I be many, may I be reproduced. He performed tapas. Having performed tapas, he created all this.' The year as the 'body' of Prajāpati means: the rhythms of nature (spring growth, summer heat, autumn harvest, winter rest) are the breathing of the cosmic creator. When you experience a season, you are experiencing a limb of Prajāpati.

sk: मासो वै प्रजापतिस्तस्य कृष्णपक्ष एव रयिः शुक्लः प्राणस्तस्मादेत ऋषयः शुक्ले इष्टं कुर्वन्तीतर उ इतरस्मिन् ||
ro: māsaḥ · vai · prajāpatiḥ · tasya · kṛṣṇa-pakṣaḥ · eva · rayiḥ · śuklaḥ · prāṇaḥ · tasmāt · ete · ṛṣayaḥ · śukle · iṣṭaṁ · kurvanti · itare · u · itarasmin ||
hi: मास (महीना) ही प्रजापति है; उसका कृष्णपक्ष (अमावस्या की ओर) रयि है; शुक्लपक्ष (पूर्णिमा की ओर) प्राण है। इसलिए ये ऋषि शुक्लपक्ष में यज्ञ करते हैं; अन्य (सामान्य) लोग इतर (कृष्णपक्ष) में।
en: The month indeed is Prajāpati; its dark half (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa) is Rayi; the bright half (śukla-pakṣa) is Prāṇa. Therefore these sages perform sacrifice in the bright half; others perform in the other (dark) half.

ws.e: the month — the lunar month, the basic unit of Vedic calendrical reckoning

ws.h: कृष्णपक्ष — अमावस्या की ओर का पखवाड़ा
ws.e: the dark fortnight — kṛṣṇa (dark) + pakṣa (wing/half); the fifteen days from full moon to new moon, when the moon wanes
the bright (fortnight) — the fifteen days from new moon to full moon, when the moon waxes; associated with growth, light, consciousness

ws.h: यज्ञ करते हैं / इष्ट-कर्म करते हैं
